Fact-check report · Relationships / Matchmaking

A dating statistic,
traced back to its source

"Men aged 25-35 with no house or car have a 12% matchmaking success rate; with a house, 45%." This claim is repeated endlessly in short videos and self-media, precise down to a single digit, and sounds like the conclusion of a real report. This page takes it apart and traces every element back to its source.

Claim under review: No house/car 12% vs house 45% First circulated: 2026-09-16 Finding: No traceable source; the direction is supported
01

The claim to be checked

The two numbers as given in the original self-media post, and the source it claims.

12%

Men with no house or car
Matchmaking success rate

→
45%

After buying a house
Matchmaking success rate

Alleged source: "Data from a certain matchmaking platform"— yet not a single element in this sentence can be traced back:
Platform not named No report title No publication year No sample size No statistical definition
02

What the check found

Two things are true at once: the numbers cannot be traced, and several mutually conflicting versions of the same phenomenon exist.

No traceable source

No original report found anywhere online

12% and 45% appear only in self-media articles, always as vague "a certain platform" citations. No named matchmaking platform has published any original report, press release or data page. In the chain of circulation these numbers have only downstream, no upstream.

Same phenomenon · different numbers

Versions of the same claim differ several-fold

Several mutually incompatible precise figures circulate about "the effect of a house on matchmaking". Each uses a different definition, yet every one is presented as a statistical conclusion.

Number comparison

Side-by-side comparison of circulating versions

The bar lengths below only show how the numbers contradict each other;they are not comparable— their denominators and definitions are entirely different.

Matchmaking success rate after buying a house45%
Definition: unknown · Source: unnamed platform
Matchmaking success rate with no house or car12%
Definition: unknown · Source: unnamed platform
House + car vs no house65% / under 10%
Definition: unknown · directly conflicts with 12% / 45%
With a house is "higher" than without62%
A relative increase — not the same kind of quantity as the percentages above
Families directly reject men without a house90%
The subject shifts from "the person's own outcome" to "the family's attitude" — the definition changes again
Conclusion: Versions of the same phenomenon differ several-fold, so these precise figures are not credible. They look more likea "directional fact"packaged asa "precise statistic"— the direction may be right, but the digits after the decimal point are invented.
03

Facts that can be verified

Failing to trace 12% and 45% does not mean the sentence describes something false. Directionally, real data does support it.

Named source
67%/48%

67% of respondents insisted on "buying a house before marrying"; 48% of men considered a house the foremost condition for marriage. China News Service, 2013

Academic survey
42.7%

42.7% of surveyed villages reported a serious problem of older unmarried men. Central China Normal University · Huang Zhenhua research group · 2024 survey
Sample: 26 provinces, 119 villages, 1,785 rural households

At the level of observable reality
The direction holds

Reports from matchmaking corners across the country show that men without a house are screened out first; property is treated as the core signal of economic strength and stability. What is reproducible is the ranking, not the percentage

Keep the two kinds of information apart:"A house is a hard threshold in the matchmaking market"is a verifiable directional judgement;"a 12% success rate"is a precise figure with no traceable source. Accepting the former does not require believing the latter.
04

How to check a statistic yourself

This process does not depend on the topic of relationships — it works for any "data shows" claim.

  1. Who is the source?"A certain platform" is not a source. A named institution, company or research team is.
  2. What is the report called, and in what year was it published?If the report name and year cannot be stated, it usually means the report does not exist.
  3. How large was the sample, and how was it drawn?1,785 rural households is a sample you can question; "data shows" is not.
  4. What are the numerator and denominator?For "matchmaking success rate", is the denominator registered users, people who met, or successful matches? Change the definition once and the number changes several-fold.
  5. Can the original document be found?Only primary sources count (papers, press releases, official statistics); second-hand retellings, screenshots and AI summaries do not.
